utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today is Thursday. I'd like to greet the accused, the Defence counsel, the OTP representatives as well as everybody assisting us. I'd like to greet the witness, Mr. Primorac, as well. I hope this will be the last day of his testimony. Very quickly I'd like to turn to the Prosecution concerning the motion to add documents on the 65 ter list. Mr. Karnavas talked about it yesterday, 1D 2941, 2942, 2943, 2944, 2945, 2946, 2947, 2948, and 2949, does the Prosecution oppose that motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning to all those around the courtroom. Your Honour, we do not oppose the motion now. As I've said before, we'll continue to reserve our position on a case-by-case basis. I do have to state a general concern while I understand the -- again, the realities of the situation, the Prosecution does have some concern that there's a continuing flow of new materials seemingly with each witness that are not previously listed and while we do not object on this occasion, it is something that we will continue to look at. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I suppose that the other Defence teams had no objection to raise either concerning the fact that those new documents will be added to the 65 ter list. Having said that, as far as time is concerned, according to our calculations, the Prosecutor still has two hours and 30 minutes. The Bench will try and refrain from asking questions in order to allow the Prosecutor to finish cross-examination. I hope there will be some redirect in the remaining time and I hope that the witness will be able to leave after this hearing and not be forced to stay until next week. I was a little too long and I will now give the floor to Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Primorac. Yesterday, we left off and we were discussing the workings of the Ministry of Finance and where we ended yesterday was determining that beneath you there was a whole structure of assistants and directors each with his or her own network of officers beneath them. Now, if we could just continue with this for a very short while. Is it correct that you as the Minister of Finance would implement government decisions taken at your level through that network downwards?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Finance implemented government decisions. That was a normal thing to do. In an operative sense, everything was done on a case-by-case basis. For the most part, the ministry was headquartered in Sarajevo in the government offices and that's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. And I think it also goes without saying that your subordinates reported back to you on their activities so that you would have a broad overview and oversight or knowledge of what was going on in your ministry.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if we move up to the level of the cabinet, am I also correct in -- if I said that similarly, you would take your direction from the prime minister as head of the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One couldn't quite put it that way. I had to operate under the laws that applied in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Understandably, whenever those laws had to be applied, there would be consultations at government level, perhaps consultations with the prime minister or with whoever happened to be at the time in charge of coordinating all these ministries. But my responsibility was to the law itself. There was no hierarchy in that way in the sense of the prime minister having the powers to give me an order that transcended my understanding of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. I think the operative word, and I picked it up in some of the documents as well, is that the various ministries obviously had to coordinate what they were doing in order for the government to function properly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just repeat this to be perfectly accurate. There was coordination between ministries that dealt with the economics and this included the Ministry of Finance. Prlic [as interpreted] headed this because he was the government's coordinator for the economy. The coordination body was coordinating all these various positions not necessarily all of the ministries accepted this. Whenever there was any misunderstandings between the ministries and the coordination body then there would be the government to deal with these. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] There is an error in the transcript. The witness said Mr. Turajlic and line 3, page 4, line 3 says Prlic. I was in that position but that was in back in 1989 and 1990 and not at the time we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you to Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Doctor, is it indeed correct that you did not mean to -- well, you didn't actually refer to Mr. Prlic but to Mr. Turajlic as he has just indicated?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, yesterday, you said that at some stage you had decided that you did not want to be minister any longer. When did you so decide actually, if you think back?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I decided that I would not be part of the new reconstructed government. If I may just remind you, on the 10th of November, 1992, the new prime minister was appointed. Until the 23rd of December, 1992, or at least that's what I assume, he was busy reshuffling the government. He invited me to become a member of this new government to get involved and my decision was not to join. I think I took my final decision sometime in mid-December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The new prime minister, that was Mr. Akmadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, while you were in Zagreb, from basically sometime in September onwards, is it -- well, first of all, is it correct that at some stage after you went on your trip to Washington, you then ended up in Zagreb and didn't return to Sarajevo for the rest of the year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Having left Sarajevo on the 18th of September, 1992, heading the republican delegation off to a conference of the World Bank until the 23rd of July, 1997 [as interpreted], I no longer returned to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure about the year that the witness mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An intervention, there is yet another interpretation error.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes, could you indicate to us?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there is yet another interpretation error. It reads here that I left Sarajevo on the 18th of September, 1992, which is true and that I never returned until the 23rd of December, 1997, and here it reads the 23rd of July, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, in the period that you had left Sarajevo, so from September until the 10th of November when Mr. Pelivan was still the prime minister, did you receive any guidance from Mr. Pelivan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Kruger. We have a problem with the transcript. The witness corrected and mentioned the 23rd of December, 1997 [as interpreted], but we still have the 23rd of July, 1997. There was a mistake in the interpretation of my words as well. The witness mentioned the 23rd of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So just to be absolutely clear, sir, from the 18th of September, it was October, November, December, so another three months or so that you were -- before you were back in Sarajevo. Or actually you did not return to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my term of office, the remaining three months, I was not in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I think we've got that clear now. Now, sir, during the first period that we're now referring to when Mr. Pelivan was still the prime minister, during that period when you were not in Sarajevo, did you receive any guidance from Mr. Pelivan regarding your duties or responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I physically met Mr. Pelivan at the time in Zagreb. I physically met him, twice, maybe three times. I'm sure about twice though. He was away from Sarajevo on business and of course when we met, I discussed with him my work and my programme. In an operative sense I was in touch with the government through Mr. Turajlic, truth to tell, in whatever way that proved possible at the time, sometimes by phone, it was difficult but sometimes possible or else we would exchange written notes. I wrote notes to Mr. Pelivan, I still keep those, as well as to Mr. Akmadzic after he took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Pelivan express any concern that you were not in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Pelivan knew what I was doing in Zagreb. He asked me to wrap up the Zagreb business as quickly as possible in order to go back. As I said yesterday when I was answering Mr. Karnavas's questions, I decided to go back to Sarajevo in late October but don't hold me to it. I can't keep all these dates in mind. It's been 15 or 16 years. I think it was in late October. Mr. Turajlic told me to postpone this trip in order to go to the EU to participate in the survival talks, the talks surrounding the so-called survival programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm told that on page 6, line 25 and page 7, line 1 the witness indicated that he wrote information to Mr. Pelivan not notes. I think there is a distinction between providing information versus notes. Perhaps we can get a clarification on that to which we have an accurate transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, to Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Dr. Primorac, you heard what Mr. Karnavas has said. Could you comment on that? Is it indeed just notes or information?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can use my documents to furnish proof. It was information, detailed information on my whereabouts, what I did at least as far as it could have been any interest to the prime minister. I would inform him about my contacts, any talks that I held. I suggested decisions for the government to be made for me to press on. Meanwhile, I had spent most of my time working, pushing forward for Bosnia and Herzegovina to join the international monetary fund, the European fund and the succession of the former Yugoslavia. All of these jobs required a lot of preparation, a lot of information and being familiar with all the documents. This was a draining job especially --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the witness please be asked to repeat the latter half of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters have difficulty in following you. They asked if you could repeat the last half of your response.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the jobs that I did required a lot of preparation, a lot of documents, a lot of information. Needless to say, given the working conditions I had in Zagreb, I didn't have any of those. I had to make an enormous effort to retrieve information, to make sure that the information that I sent on to the prime minister was thorough and complete in the sense of knowing what I was to do and in the sense of the government giving me assistance with completing -- in terms of helping me complete my own tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I need to correct the transcript. I don't know whether it's translation or whether it's the way it's been typed out. It says here on line 8, page 8, line 3, that "the European fund and the succession of the Prosecution." I know that the gentleman didn't say that because one has nothing to do with the other so I don't know where that came -- again, we want to make sure we have a clean record so perhaps if the gentleman could speak slower, maybe enunciate and then maybe we can also try to be as accurate on the other end as well. Thank you. And I'm not trying to cast aspersions to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, before it goes off the screen right at the top it says, "the European fund and the succession of the Prosecution." What were you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat what I said. I worked on jobs that had to do with Bosnia and Herzegovina as a new state being included in the World Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the International Monetary Fund, the European Bank reconstruction and development, and in jobs to do with the succession of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, the written communications that you sent to the prime minister, how were those transmitted? How did you get them to him physically?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may be an unusual term or phrase but let me answer like this: I did this in all sorts of ways. Sometimes it was by courier, there were no official couriers. There were people who travelled to Sarajevo on UNPROFOR planes or they would be coming back from Sarajevo. Normally, those people would pass through the Zagreb office and I always took the opportunity to send the information along with them. Sometimes when satellite phone lines were introduced, it was possible to talk by telephone and more often than not I used this phone line to talk to Mr. Turajlic because it had more to do with what we were doing and it was easier for us to understand each other. It was simpler. Sometimes there were cases where I was able to send a fax which I did whenever I could. Therefore, any form of communication that was available was used for exchanging information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When Mr. Akmadzic succeeded Mr. Pelivan, did you continue this form of communication with him as well?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, much in the same way as before. I still have documents like that in my file. However, I do have to digress a little when we come to speak of that particular communication between me and him. Pelivan was an economist and Akmadzic was not an economist, therefore, Akmadzic would normally refer me to Mr. Turajlic for any coordination with the government because he was in charge of coordinating the work of this particular ministry, however, I do have documents that I sent to Akmadzic in my files that I still keep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to turn to a subject which I know is sensitive to you and I do not do this at all to try and embarrass you. I'd like to refer you to Prosecution document P 10467. P 10467. So, this is a transcript of an audio recording of the -- of the 178th Session of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency and this was held on the 21st of December, 1992. Do you have the document before you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, at this meeting, the -- one of the main topics of discussion was -- can be summed up if you look at the first place where the president speaks and it's just after Mile Akmadzic, so the president says, "So let's make a change here, namely, with the ministers of national defence, finance, the minister of transport ..." et cetera, do you have that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, can I use pencil and secondly, can I scribble notes all over this copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please direct me again to the relevant paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I think it would be on your first page and it is the first place where the president speaks and he says, "So let's make a change here, namely, the minister of finance -- national defence, finance ..." do you have that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My text reads as follows. "Those are the ministries that were before and there is nothing else then ..." is that what I'm supposed to find?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, it would be on the first page.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You have it.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I've only just noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So you see that you are also under discussion here or your position and there is talk of making a change. Now, sir, at this period, you were also of course not in Sarajevo, you were still in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, at the bottom of page 3 in the English, and it is also page 3 in the B/C/S version -- I wonder if it is page 3. It is where Mr. Mile Akmadzic speaks -- sorry, if we can go just a bit above that where Mr. Ejup Ganic speaks and Mr. Ejup Ganic says, "Let's say a minister has been absent three or four months and nobody at the ministry can do a thing because of the minister's absence." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, this applies to you in the sense that you were one of the ministers who was absent for three months at that stage. How did your ministry function during your absence?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a deputy in Sarajevo and he ran the ministry in my absence, at least as far as the work that was actually going on in Sarajevo was concerned. And then I tried to explain about the jobs that can only be done outside Sarajevo, all right, so I was in charge of those. I can't be unfair and say that the ministry did not suffer at all because the minister was away. Those were sensitive jobs, that much is certain. However, I don't think that Ganic's statement here makes any other sense aside from its use as propaganda because this same Mr. Ganic travelled with me throughout Europe while I was the finance minister of BH. He was presenting government programmes for collecting supplies and stuff to do with the survival programme that was meant to ensure the physical survival of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just before we move on. I see that the president speaks next and then Mr. Akmadzic speaks. And he says, "I propose," this is talking about the replacement ministers or the new candidates. "I propose four ethnic Croatian candidates, the ones to be proposed by the HDZ. I received the obligation and they were at the HDZ. In fact, only Primorac was not at the HDZ." Sir, the fact that you were not a member of the HDZ, did that at all hamper you in the performance of your duties within this government?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally speaking, no, because the government functioned as an executive body of the Presidency and at the government meetings, no decisions were taken on the proposals based on the membership in certain political party but essentially, I didn't have available political information that could have helped me in my work because I had no contact with the HDZ which in this particular instance represented the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, at the top of the next page, that would be the next page in the English -- sorry. It's page 5, I'm afraid. It's the president speaking. He speaks just after Mr. Pejanovic and the president then says, "Is the finance minister present? Really, we have three cases. I don't know even Primorac is absent rightfully, is he? I don't know. You know better." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Kruger, I'm sorry but you said page 5. I do not find -- that particular quotation, I do not find on page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: On the top of this page -- yes, okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's page 5 of 8, yes. Sorry. I missed for a moment as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just after that, Mr. Ganic says, "No, he is not back yet, he has been ordered to come back." Then Mr. Akmadzic said: "I gave the order, I said if he wants to be in the government." Now, sir, did Mr. Akmadzic contact you around this time?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic talked to me on several occasions while we were physically in contact when he was out of Sarajevo and I believe that he called me once by telephone from Sarajevo but I cannot confirm this definitely. So he called me once again and proposed that I come back and become a member of the government and as I told you earlier, I had decided not to join the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Ganic, when he says that you have been ordered back, can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how Mr. Ganic could possibly know that. He was not my superior and as far as I can remember, he never talked about this subject with me although we were on the road for days. And I explained earlier and I can repeat it again, once I decided to come back after being persuaded -- after the president of the government tried to persuade me and why I didn't go back I can explain again, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just before moving on with this document, do you recall yesterday when the Court was looking at Defence Exhibit 1D 02696, and I don't think you need to go into it, this was the work programme of the staff in gathering funds for the needs of the population of the RBiH until 30 September 1992; do you remember that work programme? Now, in that work programme, I saw at least two items where you and Mr. Ganic would act together, one was item 5, and that said "Present project to the ECC with Ganic." And item 12 which was to hold talks with the USA and Canada with inter alia Mr. Ganic. Do you recall that that was on the programme?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would be grateful if you could be to the right of the microphone.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this item being on the agenda or part of the programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can just quickly move all my stuff for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, with that in mind, if we can turn to the last page of Exhibit P 10467, these are the minutes of the 21st of December and this is where Mr. Ganic speaks again. In the very first part, Mr. Ganic says the following: "Some positions in the government are empty. Zarko Primorac and I were supposed to go to America on 20 September. I was not able to but he left there on 14 September and never came back. We went to Brussels together for a single day. I came back." Now, first of all, this trip to America, that was the one which was listed in the work programme; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me first to read this in order to comprehend the entirety of it. First of all, it is not correct that Ganic and I were planned to travel to America on the 20th September. According to the programme of the government for collecting funds, it is true that he and I were appointed to hold talks in America and Canada by the 30th of September, 1992. There was no precise date for our travel, nor had any meetings were organised prior to that. Secondly, I did not leave on the 14th of September to America but I went after the 20th of September. I left Sarajevo for Zagreb on the 18th of September and two or three days later after that, I went to America. I think that the World Bank assembly and the IMF was held on the 25th or the 26th of September, 1992. I headed the BiH delegation. I did not go to America based on the government programme in order to hold talks relating to the collection of funds but rather, I went on the instruction of the government as the head of the delegation of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the annual assembly meeting of the bank and the fund and Mr. Ganic was not involved in these talks and I am afraid that he is mixing up things here but that's his problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just after that, but the fourth line it goes on, he says, "Therefore, these people who went up there, they broke every norm. Believe me, the news will be very well received if we say that we have replaced six ministers who were failing to show up at work." Now, from this, it seems to me that within the cabinet, not everybody was aware of the functions that you were performing as prime minister -- sorry, as finance minister, my correction. Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that for the simple reason that I informed about my work the officials who were relating to me or had connections with me. What they did with that afterwards, I am not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just returning for a moment to that work programme, there were three other items on the work programme which was 1D 02696, where you also had assignments -- and you needn't go into them and I would just ask you whether you recall. There was an item which said you had to hold talks with Austria, did you hold any talks with Austria?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Vienna and talked to a law firm because I had been assigned, given an assignment by the government among other things to open a bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Vienna in order to take care of international financial transactions so I initiated talks with a law firm in Vienna to prepare the necessary documents so these are the contacts that I had in Vienna. I had no contacts, however, with any government authorities of the republic of Austria.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can move to the Presidency meeting which was held on the next day, and that was the 22nd of December. This would be Prosecution Exhibit P 10496. If you can turn to the B/C/S version. Now, on the -- on page 6 of 8 in the English version, and this would be where Mr. Akmadzic speaks again, and it says, "Zarko Primorac is not in Sarajevo now for three months." Do you have that section?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at page 6. I see that Akmadzic has spoken. Can you please tell me how it begins in English and then I'll find my way through?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: "Zarko Primorac is not in Sarajevo now for three months." Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet. [In English] I have on page 6, I have Akmadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the -- sorry. If you look at the -- oh, my goodness. I'm afraid that I didn't check that in the B/C/S transcript. Sir, if I could read to you what it says, there are only short pieces, I would just like your comments on this. Mr. Akmadzic says: "Zarko Primorac is not in Sarajevo now for three months." Now, we know that that is accurate at that stage. Mr. Filipovic, he speaks next and at the end of what he says, he says, "Excuse me, we had situations that certain ministers had never submitted a single report to the parliament." Now, sir, would that apply to you as finance minister during the three months that you were absent?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to make certain corrections if you allow me, I apologise. I am relying on what you have read and at the time there was no parliament, there was a Presidency. The parliament was not working for the simple reason that it could not convene. Secondly, as a rule, ministers do not submit any reports to a parliament but rather inform the government about their work and it is the government that communicates with the parliament. Thirdly, I have dozens of documents, information and other papers that I sent to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, this remark of Mr. Filipovic has no relevance and is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I have actually located where this would be in your version. If you look at the top right-hand corner, you will see a big number, 0180 and then if you can find the number which ends with 6590?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could someone please assist me with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I do have a loose version of it for you if that would help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While this is happening, I trust my friend will also be going into page 7 where Mr. Akmadzic validates what Mr. Primorac testified under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the only reason I show this to you is you see that Mr. Akmadzic speaks and he says, "Only one thing, all who know me know also that Zarko Primorac is my personal friend and friend of the family, please, and now let me tell you that Zarko Primorac told me that he does not want to be in Sarajevo, that he does not want to be in the government and those of you who had heard something you did not hear it well." Sir, that just confirms what you said earlier that you had decided that you did not want to continue in the government?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm glad that Mr. Akmadzic has said that but still I can't find this piece of text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You heard -- did you hear the translation well and you understood? I think if you turn the page, perhaps, sir. It doesn't matter. You can confirm what I've just said, that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind since I was trying to find this particular piece of text, could you please read it to me out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. Akmadzic: "Only one thing. All who know me know also that Zarko Primorac is my personal friend and friend of the family." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: "Please and now let me tell you that Zarko Primorac told me that he does not want to be in Sarajevo, that he does not want to be in the government." That's correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I had told him that I did not want to be in the government. I repeated that several times. At the time I wasn't objectively able to be in Sarajevo and I can explain why. First of all, my flat was devastated and soon after that, I was dismissed from my position in Energoinvest company and therefore I had to look for a job some place else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can very briefly just turn to -- this would be a Defence Exhibit 1D 01632 and if I could ask the usher to perhaps provide the binder to the witness again. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is the document which basically, if I recall correctly, it settles up the final -- the financial obligations towards you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is some misunderstanding obviously. The gentleman has given me a completely different document and I have before me the decision to relieve and appoint ministers -- members of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that's I have in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Well, while you have that in front you, sir, yesterday you said that you did not like the word that they used in that. So could you perhaps just tell us why they were using the one word but you prefer the other, this is this dismiss and relieve thing?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my mind, it has nothing to do with sacking or in Croatia, it says that they are relieved of their duties which just simply means that they cease to be ministers. This is a normal procedure when you have a reshuffling of the government. Some ministers for various reasons cease to be ministers and the usual term that is used and I think quite rightly and correctly is that these gentlemen were relieved from their duties rather than being sacked or dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I'd like to refer you and this is back in the Prosecution binder to P 10503. P 10503. P 10503.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] 0503.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please tell me which particular document is in question? In front of me, I have P 10503, there's obviously some confusion. Is that the right document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It is a Belgrade Politika article of 12 October 1992. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the -- I don't want to spend lots of time on this document, it's not hugely important, but this is also an article about members of the Bosnia and Herzegovina government not being in Sarajevo and then if you look about halfway through the article, it says, "In this way, Sarajevo ceases to be the centre and becomes a deserted city." Do you have that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It begins "Thereby, Sarajevo will become a deserted place."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: "And many members of the government have already left it but given the fact that they have been given a deadline for returning, the city on the Miljacka is the scene of political disagreements, aside from the military conflict." "In the difficult times of war," next paragraph, "it is almost humourous to note that no one is hiding from the fact that there is not a single government in the world aside from the Bosnian Herzegovinian one that has the headquarters of its ministries in foreign states." Do you have any brief comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may object at this point. I don't see the relevance of this. That's number one. Number two, there has been testimony with respect to provisos in the constitution that would allow, based on the All People's Defence, for instance for government offices for relocated in a time of war. Now, I don't want to go into this but I don't see the relevance. The gentleman has already indicated the reasons why. Yesterday, he told us based on the financial institutions he needed means of communications, his flat was deserted, was desecrated or destroyed and so on so forth. We've heard testimony from others. I don't see pulling out a newspaper from Belgrade, from Belgrade of all places, that Politika was the mouthpiece of the Belgrade government to somehow have a discussion here. Now, if we want to have a political discourse, that's fine, but we're here to determine some discrete issues on law, not to have a discussion of what Politika, this Belgrade government mouthpiece had to say at the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't belabour this point. I think the point has already been made by the witness. There is one other thing that I would, from this article, just like to inquire from the witness, that is towards the end of the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It says, "Prime Minister Jure Pelivan, also from the HDZ," do you have that paragraph? It's probably -- about the fourth paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: "Prime Minister Jure Pelivan, also from the HDZ, is in Sarajevo together with vice-presidents, Miodrag Simovic, Zarko Primorac and Rusmir Mahmutcehajic." Is that a mistake because this article comes from October of 1992? You weren't in Sarajevo at that stage, just to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's certainly a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just the next sentence, "Does anyone remember Franjo Boras and recall that he is still officially a member of the BH Presidency." Mr. Boras was he still active in government at this stage?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boras was never in government. He was a member of the BH Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And was he still active as a member of the BH Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, before stepping on to a new topic, one final thing that I'd just like to ask you. From your testimony, it seems that during your period away from Sarajevo, the last three months of your tenure, you had more dealings with Mr. Turajlic than with Mr. Pelivan.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't physically measure that. It's impossible. Where I tried to explain about the nature of my job objectively speaking, the work of the ministry of finance had more to do with coordinating the economy. Likewise, I have to say that at least twice if not more I physically met Jure Pelivan in Zagreb and discussed my job with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's step on to a new topic and what I would like to explore now with you is the whole issue of the currency and currencies being used in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, the first thing that I'd like to ask of you, and this is simply because I don't know how these things work, I'm not an economist or have very little idea of finance but as a minister of finance, would it be one of your responsibilities to protect the value of the official currency?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't protect a currency by state decree. It has to be its objective value and the objective value of a currency is driven by the economy behind it. It is true that there are measures that a country can take in order to try and preserve the value of its currency and its purchasing power. This is normally referred to as monetary policies and this is something that the central bank of any country is normally in charge of. The government or the Minister of Finance try to maintain stability by maintaining a balance in a country's economy between the production and consumption, between the various sectors such as private and public. The minister of finance is not directly responsible for a currency's stability but he is a member of a government and any government will try to contribute to a country's stability and the stability of the country's currency always goes some way towards guaranteeing the stability of a country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So as a minister of finance, you would also work closely with the central bank to attempt to at least ensure some stability in this regard?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to bring one thing up. The central bank is an independent institution by virtue of its nature; it's independent from the government. Were this not the case, the government could always end up spending a lot more than it should. There is no government that doesn't wish to spend more in addition to the fact the central bank was independent and was answerable to the parliament and not the government it was true that there was a degree of coordination between the ministry of finance and the bank. More often than not, there wasn't a lot of understanding shown between the two. They would be at logger heads more often than not, the ministry wanted to spend as much as possible and the bank wanted to spend as little as possible in order to preserve the stability of the currency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: During your tenure as finance minister, the governor of the bank was Mr. Stiepo Andrijic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the levels of currency, would it be the responsibility of the central bank or would you also have an interest in ensuring that there is sufficient currency or cash in circulation in a country and not too much?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the principal task of the central bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This task, just to understand it, perhaps, does that entail that if there is too much currency in circulation, that that means too much buying power and too few goods to go around? How does that work? Why is that important?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's important in order to keep the prices stable within the country and this makes sure that the whole system remains stable. Are there conditions for inflation, for example? That's normally when prices go up, that's what you call it and this is no use to anyone. The central bank in its own policies and in its projected policies sets certain rules by saying, over the next year, I will use these channels or those channels to put so much money into circulation in a bid to maintain some sort of a balance. Normally, there is a council of governors or a national bank council that approves this. In this regard, they are independent institutions, true enough, but they are under an obligation to submit annual reports on their work to the country's parliament and the parliament says this is good or this is no good and they only answer to the parliament. Again, I'm saying at an operative level there has been coordination between the government and the bank, nonetheless, the bank remains independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And is it also important to keep control over the levels of foreign currency in a particular state in a country?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously. Any central bank is not only responsible for preserving stability within a country in terms of domestic currency. It is also responsible for ensuring liquidity in terms of foreign currency, as they say. It must make ensure that the country and all its subjects are able to make foreign payments or pay for any commitments which means that they need to have projected foreign policies in terms of foreign currency. Okay, it is in this field that we did a lot more cooperation with the ministry than elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, I picked up, sir, somewhere that you used a very interesting simile and is it correct that there must be confidence in a currency and you said it's kind of like a religion, you need confidence in the religion to believe in it. I suppose my question is: Is confidence in the currency an important factor?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would call that paramount especially in today's conditions when all the currencies, all the world's currencies are just paper but there's no internal value. The paper is only worth what it's used for and the paper is only used in currency because it is rubber stamped by a certain country, the country then goes on to say this is our currency, this is how payments are made. Psychological factors are of paramount importance in the monetary world, expectations, confidence and so on and so forth. Confidence in a currency is a paramount factor in determining its value.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, with that as a basis, in time of war as you were facing the situation you were in as finance minister, is it correct that there was indeed a shortage of cash in Bosnia and Herzegovina or currency, rather?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite the contrary, we had too much cash. I'll try to explain this. While the Yugoslav dinar was still in circulation as the official currency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnia and Herzegovina as a country couldn't get away from that channel of monetary supply. We would get our money from Yugoslavia's central bank. The dinar was affected by galloping inflation and the presses were working at full tilt producing money 24 hours a day. The denominations kept getting bigger and bigger and there was more and more money. We tried to protect ourselves from this, and I do have a document to this effect, from this flood of money coming from outside the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina by ordering that all the bank notes of the former Yugoslavia be stamped one day, that they be marked. Wherever -- may I continue, please? So these bank notes were marked or stamped whenever possible. But this didn't help stem the flood of money from outside because I think they produced these stamps elsewhere too, and when using them, we realised that this measure was to no avail. And then finally, we decided to introduce our own money. Although I might say that, at the time, this was a political decision and this political decision to introduce BH money was made before I became a member of the government and then I operationalised the idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. Kruger. Witness, I didn't want to intervene but I don't understand what you mean. Yesterday, you said there was no money left to the point when you had to bring some but the UNPROFOR couldn't guarantee the delivery so you used coupons. Today, you're saying that there was too much cash in circulation. Maybe I misunderstood what you said. Could you help me understand better your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about a period when Bosnia and Herzegovina and its monetary system were still connected to the Yugoslav dinar and Yugoslavia's central national bank, that is Belgrade, that's before our own BH money was introduced. I was talking about a period when large amounts of cash were coming in from that source and being devalued all the time. What you're talking about, Your Honour, is something that is about later on when we decided to print our own money but we could not bring it into Bosnia because UNPROFOR refused to help us with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, sir, when the BiH dinar was introduced, the Yugoslav dinar was then basically -- was the Yugoslav dinar a problem or the flood of the Yugoslav dinars, was that to a certain extent aggressed or the problems created by the flood?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't think I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When the BiH dinar was introduced on the 17th of August of 1992, it was introduced at a level of 1:10 in relation to the Yugoslav dinar. Did that to a certain extent regress the problem with this flood of Yugoslav dinars coming in and creating problems?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe in part and maybe at first. I have to tell you more about what the situation really was. The BH dinar was introduced as the official BH currency, the objective being to achieve circulation throughout BH territory. But we couldn't bring it into Sarajevo and we used coupons in Sarajevo, rather, the bank had it replaced by coupons. You remember perhaps yesterday we read that decision by the national bank, the coupons were only valid throughout Sarajevo's territory. In other parts of the Republic of B & H as the Yugoslav dinar had been invalidated, the remaining territories were now without a currency. They did whatever they could. Some printed their own coupons, some used German mark and someone used something else, therefore the situation was very complex. Back to your question about the BH dinar, did that help stop the flood of money that was coming from Belgrade. That was only at first, but very soon this new currency was affected by inflation as well and it only existed as money that was actually used for no more than a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, how does it happen then that in addition to the official currency, certain other currencies as, for instance, the Deutschemark becomes a currency of use in a particular area?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Deutschemark was a much loved currency in Bosnia and Herzegovina and throughout the former Yugoslavia before its break-up owing to the fact that this was a stable currency and owing to the fact that a lot of migrant workers from Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia worked in Germany made sure there was a steady supply of those to the Yugoslav market. This was a situation where there was no other currency available so people tried to use whatever they had for their payments. To all practical intents, late in 1992 and early 1993, in Bosnia and Herzegovina or at least the part that I'm talking about, one used cash more often than not, one used the Deutschemark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So the use of the Deutschemark was a pragmatic occurrence or it was dictated by the circumstances as it were?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was something that was a result of the circumstances that prevailed, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: To make the dinar an acceptable currency to use, would it have to be cleared with the central bank in cooperation with the finance ministry, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained yesterday about the introduction of the BH dinar. First, at some level of the Presidency there was a political decision to replace the Yugoslav one and introduce the new BH dinar. And then at government level when I was a minister in that government, the law was passed on this new currency saying the former Yugoslavia's currency was now no longer valid and now we had a new currency issued by the BH national bank and there were regulations about it and a whole lot of other things, too. Then the national bank, because that's what it did, implemented this by actually getting the money printed and putting it into circulation wherever possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But in order for the Deutschemark, for instance, to be legal tender with -- on the territory of the -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina in cash transactions, would the central government need to know about this or have some involvement and make it legal or acceptable?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Deutschemark was never officially recognised as Bosnia and Herzegovina's currency. It was used before the war for the purposes of something that one could have described as the black market or the grey market, if you like. According to foreign currency regulations that applied before the war, anyone coming into possession of the Deutschemark or any other foreign currency under the rules of the game had to have that currency exchanged for the Yugoslav dinar because that was the currency used for payments in the former Yugoslavia. Nevertheless, where monetary issues are concerned, the market always follows its own logic. People would keep the Deutschemark. People would have savings in Deutschemark, in foreign currency. Unfortunately, that came to nothing later on but people tried to put themselves in the safe side as it were. There was a lot of cash flowing where the Deutschemark was used before the war, but once the war began, this grew and was now on a massive scale because there was no other currency to be used. It was never official apart from some areas but just to make one thing perfectly clear, Deutschemark was never at any point in time recognised as the official currency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was it at any stage officially recognised as a -- we could perhaps call it a parallel currency in addition to the BiH dinar for pragmatic purposes?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me about Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole, and the government, and if you're inquiring about the period of time during which I worked as minister, the answer is no, it was never recognised as a parallel currency. I was vaguely aware of such cases outside of Sarajevo in some areas, in some areas that recognised the Deutschemark as their official currency but it only pertained to those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if -- in order to recognise, for instance, the Deutschemark as a parallel currency in Bosnia and Herzegovina, would it have been necessary to coordinate this with the German authorities, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you a general answer. Whenever you are introducing a foreign currency in your own country, you must have authorisation from the country where this currency is originally used. The reasons are both theoretical and practical. If you take someone else's money and you now recognise it as your own you must have a source available to you and what is the source? The source is obviously the country where this currency is officially used, produced and printed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... to intervene but it's a very technical subject. It seems to me that the role of the World Bank, of the International Monetary Fund, the IMF, must have had consequences on the currency in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You told us that you attended some meetings of the IMF. So what was the position of the IMF towards your currency? Did you receive recommendations, suggestions on the way to solve that problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course those issues were debated especially with the IMF because it's the central monetary institution for international purposes, in a way. It regulates the relationships between various currencies, their values and so on and so forth. The World Bank is linked to this but not directly. It helps countries rebuild and develop thereby increasing the value of that country's currency. But let me go back to the International Monetary Fund. The former Yugoslavia broke up and there were now a number of new emerging countries, Slovenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia and Serbia and Montenegro were still together and Macedonia. These countries were not members of the IMF yet. We were talking about becoming members because we were now an independent state. The fund in principal agreed to this in political terms but they wanted us to sort out our responsibilities to the fund. The former Yugoslavia owed money to the IMF. In order for us to become a new member, we had to assume some of the commitments of the former Yugoslavia and sort this out with the fund in one way or another by simply paying back or doing something else about it. This was a torturous process allocating these debts to the former republics who owed what and such like. We could not expect any official recommendations from the fund at a time. They were in a position to make friendly suggestions, perhaps, but not to offer any official views or positions; therefore, these ongoing consultations with the IMF were something that was a matter of friendly consultations and no more than that until such time as we actually became a member of the IMF.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did they tell you? What did they suggest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The IMF is primarily interested in the stability of a country's currency and its rules stipulate conditions under which the IMF will intervene, so to speak, in a country in order not to depreciate the currency of a specific country more than what is necessary. Any devaluation of a currency exceeding 10 per cent per annum must be approved in a certain way by the IMF so their advice given to us, if I remember correctly but I have notes, was to -- if we want to introduce our currency, we should strive to maintain its stability to make it convertible as soon as possible and to introduce it into international transactions also as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Kruger, we're going to break for 20 minutes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, according to our calculations, you should have one hour and five minutes left without inflation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, sir, still on the issue of selecting a parallel currency or implementing a currency parallel to that of your own currency, if that were to be done, would the stability of the parallel currency be an issue of importance?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that I understand your question but I will try to tell you this. A country may introduce a parallel currency but, of course, always with the approval of the country whose currency is being adopted as a parallel means of payment. And quite understandably, these countries, although this is very rare nowadays, this applied much more to the time when we had coins and silver and gold but I do not rule out this possibility even nowadays. In such a situation, the country introducing a parallel currency is very much interested to preserve its own currency as well as the originating country of the parallel currency to preserve its own currency. That applies to any country in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: A government deciding to take such steps, is it safe to assume that that government would opt for a stable currency so as not to import all kinds of inflation from outside its borders suffered by a different currency?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are probably right. If anyone wishes to introduce a parallel currency, it is only reasonable to introduce a currency that is more stable than the domestic one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if I could refer you to Prosecution Exhibit P 10501. P 10501. If you can turn to the B/C/S version. This is a report of the RBiH Armed Forces Supreme Command and it's dated the 6th of September. And the title page says, "Please find attached the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Armed Forces Supreme Command Staff report on the conditions and system of financing of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Armed Forces." If we turn to the next page, the actual report, it says, "Subject -- and then the first paragraph after subject, do you have that? It says, "We hereby inform you ..." sorry, this is Sefer Halilovic who wrote this. He says, "We hereby inform you that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina National Bank has still not enabled access to the funds from the approved budget for the OS RBiH financing, armed forces financing." Did you know anything about this or about this problem?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was definitely aware that there were huge problems in financing the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I do not remember this particular document but since my name is mentioned therein and since it's dated the 4th September, 1992, I presume that I had an occasion to see it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes. Just for the record it was also addressed to you as we see on the last page, Ministry of Finance, Mr. Zarko Primorac along with Mr. Jure Pelivan and the RBiH National Bank, Mr. Stiepo Andrijic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this document was delivered to others. I see that there are four addressees. It is probably delivered to me and -- because this was a normal way of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, in the English translation, it's marked as page 4, and in your version it would be the paragraph just above where there is a whole list of figures marked in BH dinar. I'd just like to ask you about this paragraph which starts with, "As the financing system cannot keep on functioning this way ..." do you have that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: "And since the RBiH National Bank has still not signed the agreement on utilisation of the budget funds with the RBiH government, we deem that this problem needs to be solved immediately." Now, my question is it's a time of war and the defence force needs to be funded, it's probably an issue of national security or paramount national security. What was this delay, then, in signing an agreement which would release funds?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise for taking a few minutes to explain the situation because otherwise I cannot answer your question, if you allow me to give this explanation then my answer will make sense. When I became the minister there was no budget in the state because it was at war. We, if you remember, we mentioned that yesterday, we had adopted a decision on how to finance a country at war. Based on that decision, and when I say "we" I mean the government and the Presidency, we in the Ministry of Finance prepared a budget. Just like any other budget, it had the expenditure and the revenue sides. Based on the best available information at the time, we made the calculation of expenditure and -- but when we came to the sources of how to finance this expenditure, we realised that we had very little funds available because simply there were no taxes, there were no customs duties, there were no other sources of state revenues. So these expenditures could only be financed by issuing new money, that means printing money by the national bank of BH. The printing of money is a job which means that if you -- there's nothing, no commodities that you can buy with this money is a fruitless job, you are just issuing worthless paper that cannot purchase anything. We tried to explain to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina that we can -- and when I say "we" I'm also speaking on behalf of the governments of the national bank. We can issue as much money as we can with the bank notes with certain denominations but they would be useless. Okay, for a certain period of time, they accepted coupons and paid their expenditure with that for as long as there was commodities on the market to be purchased; however, when the commodities disappeared, nobody wanted to accept these coupons. Therefore, the army was right in protesting and we also could have printed as many coupons as we wanted but they also lost their value. As far as the goods were concerned, the budget was established for the period of three months, let us say until the end September. That was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we turn to -- just look at the same document, the third paragraph of the document, so just a bit above the bit that you read now. It would be on your previous page. The one to the third paragraph around about the middle, there is reference to "As well as the introduction of the Bosnia and Herzegovina dinar currency while the payment transactions in currencies that are not legal payment instruments in the territory of RBiH are being strengthened (Croatian dinar and German mark) the introduction of a single currency is prevented as well." Then it says, "The functioning of the armed forces and equipping of units' salary, payment, is delayed which is creating dissatisfaction amongst members of the armed forces. The trust in the BH currency is being lost causing the establishment of the black market exchange rate which has reached the value of 700 to 1.200 BHD for one German mark." Now, sir, the first question on this, perhaps if you could just once again comment on transactions in currencies that are not legal instruments on the territory of RBiH?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I can add anything more to what I already said but just for further clarification, under such conditions which are unstable and catastrophic, people psychologically try to turn to more valuable things. They try to have in their hands something which is of more worth. Of course the currency mentioned here, the Croatian dinar and particularly the German mark were worth more at the time than the BH currency and in that sense, the people tended to have these currency as preferable currencies. It had nothing to do with national feeling, it was pure interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to a few other documents. Let's have a look at Prosecution Exhibit P 00258. I think it would be the first document in your binder. This is a document of 15 June 1992, and it's president of the municipal Crisis Staff Josip Boro who wrote this, it's in Kiseljak, and the decision says, "The Croatian dinar is hereby introduced on the territory of the Kiseljak municipality as the currency of account. Other currencies can be used as an instrument of payment as well." My first question, I don't know this may be a translation issue but is it significant that it says "the Croatian dinar is introduced as the currency of account"?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The English says, "The Croatian dinar is introduced as the currency of account ..." and then other currencies may be used as well. I was just struck by the Croatian dinar it doesn't say is introduced as "a" currency.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are to interpret this decision literally, this decision is pointless from the point of view of monetary theory and practice but let me tell you how I understand it. They said that the Croatian dinar was introduced as a currency of account which means as the basis for calculation not a means of payment. Any currency primarily functions as a means of payment which means that every liability can be settled in this currency. There are so-called clearing currencies which are not in circulation. Let me give you an example. Before the war, the former Yugoslavia had the so-called clearing account with the USSR and the clearing currency under this agreement between the two countries was the US dollar. Therefore, the US dollar was not the currency for payment transactions between the two countries but as a kind of stable benchmark for calculating the accounts between the two countries. This is what this decision says about the Croatian dinar specifying it as a clearing currency whereas other currencies can be used as legal tenders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Still on this topic then. If we look at the next document, P 00281, the very next document in the binder. And this is a decision by Mr. Jadran Topic, president of -- or signed by him, president of the Mostar HVO and it's dated the 24th of July, 1992. It says, "This decision adopts the Croatian dinar as means of cash payment."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we go to that, just a technical issue. I'm told that our witness indicated -- and this would be on line 22 of page 40 where he talked about this is what this decision says about the Croatian dinar specifying it as a clearing currency whereas other currencies can be used as -- for payments, here it says legal tenders. I just want to make sure that we have a clear translation and a clear transcript so perhaps we can get some clarification on that or is it the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, you have heard the intervention. Could you perhaps just clarify that for us?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go back to this previous decision taken by Kiseljak municipality. It has two parts as you can see. The first sentence says that in the area of Kiseljak municipality, the Croatian dinar is being introduced as a clearing currency and as the means of payment other currencies can be used as well. And in that respect, the decision, although it's incomplete, is quite clear. The Croatian dinar serves as the clearing currency whereas the other currencies, the German mark or some others can be used as a means of payments and that's a big difference between the two. The clearing currency is not an effective currency, it just serves to settle the accounts and calculations between companies and it does not appear as the means of payment in the transactions. And as I understand the second part, other currencies were to be used to effect payments and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just before moving then to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Kruger. It just so happens -- it's a miracle but there is a French translation of the document. I don't know where it comes from. It may be done -- may have been done by CLSS but the French translation does not say that or exactly the same. I'm going to read out slowly what is written here. "The Croatian dinar is introduced as unit of account in the territory of the Kiseljak municipality. Other currencies may also be used as payment units or instruments."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters don't have the text in either language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the French version says that the Croatian dinar can be used as a unit of account but that other currencies can be used as payment instruments. So that's not quite the same thing, not quite the same as the English version. Because when you use the article "the" in front of currency, it seems to imply something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It appears that the French translation as you have read it does then also accord with what the witness has said, a unit of account or a benchmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, on this, before moving to the next document, perhaps, if a benchmark is introduced as the been done here in Kiseljak, would it make sense to choose as your benchmark a stable currency?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only guess that. I can't give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But would your guess be that if you had a choice between the German Deutschemark and the Zimbabwe dollar, which one would you choose, to make it very dramatic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would choose the better one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's move to the next document. This is P 00281. This was the president of the Mostar HVO, Mr. Jadran Topic and in this decision, 24 July, he says, "This decision adopts the Croatian dinar as means of cash payment in Mostar municipality." So my first question: This is a step further than what we saw with the previous document. This is not only setting the dinar as a benchmark or the Croatian dinar, it's making it a cash payment currency.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This decision, is this different than the Kiseljak decision which only instituted Croatian dinar as a benchmark, this decision actually institutes the Croatian dinar as a means of cash payment?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be more explicit again. Both these documents are legal documents and probably their interpretation and their legal meaning should be done by someone who is a lawyer by profession. That's the first thing. Secondly, neither of these decisions -- and please bear that in mind and I will continue from my aspect which is the monetary aspect, to try to understand these two decisions. In my view, neither of these socio-political communities as they were used to be called which are now municipalities had no any legal basis for introducing a different currency in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina; however, once they've done that, and I think there was no legal basis for that, and if that is the case, then these decisions are null and void. But from the monetary point of view, if such a decision is taken and if something is to serve as money regardless of how it is called in some other country, then this kind of decision must contain at least five stipulations and that is: First, a certain currency should be declared withdrawn and invalid. Secondly, that a new money called this and this is being introduced and that all the monetary values in the territory in or in a country shall be recalculated and translated into this new currency unit. This should also stipulate how these ratios are going to be calculated and also to specify the source of this new money. These decisions contain none of these stipulations and if you want me to compare this decision to the previous one, it means a step forward but it lost another meaning, it just says that the Croatian dinar is going to be used as means of cash payment. Money means much more than cash payment, it has other functions as well which are more important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, in light of what you have just said, could we look at the next document, that is P 00447. This is a decree signed by the president of the HVO, Dr. Jadranko Prlic and it's dated 22 September 1992. The decree is on the regulation of payment transactions in Croatian dinars on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna during the immediate threat of war or state of war. Article 1, "This decree prescribes the regulation of payment transactions in Croatian dinars ..." et cetera, et cetera. In light of what you have said with regard to the previous two documents, could you comment on this third document?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I commented yesterday in chief on this document. Again, my role is to comment and no more. I repeat what I said before in terms of its substance from a purely monetary aspect, this document is not a document based on which somewhere in some country, some territory, one could accept a different currency for making payments but I do have to make another general observation. Knowing about monetary theory and knowing about finances in general, Herceg-Bosna, the Zenica district, the Tuzla district, the Bihac district might as well not have written down a single word concerning money, might have adopted not a single document. Life would still have gone on and the same thing would have happened more likely than not. Therefore, all decisions of this kind are to some extent formal and no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, all of these -- or these three documents that we've just been talking about, were any of these documents cleared or notified to your ministry?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first two documents, I can tell you that I've never seen them before. And this document from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna office, I saw this after I left Sarajevo which may have been sometime in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday, we looked at the law regarding socio-political communities. Is it correct that decisions taken by or measures implemented by socio-political communities still had to be done in coordination with the central government?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be normal to assume that all the BH laws that applied had to be coordinated but you must bear in mind the conditions under which we worked. For months at a stretch, there would be no communication at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's have a look at document P 02663. These, sir, are minutes of the 182nd Session of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on 26th December, 1992. You have it in front of you.
