Now, if we can go to the last page of the decision, and it's also the last page in the translation -- sorry, not decision, the minutes, do you see the place where Mr. Mile Akmadzic speaks? And he says the following: "Just to say this, that the Presidency is at the same time -- of course, the government proposed this but with respect to financial help, we are in big trouble. We are practically printing money. We are in a very serious situation and I think that we will have to put this on the agenda one day. First on the government agenda and the Presidency agenda but we of course -- the economy does not work. Every such demand means devaluation." Then Ejup Ganic says, "Last time when I was there, I saw that (Croatia) the exchange rate was -- went 50 per cent up." And then Mile, I take it that would be Mile Akmadzic says, "We devaluate the Croatian currency. We devaluate the Croatian dinars, that is to say Herzegovina, the area from where the Croatian dinars comes from."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we just check the reference? It doesn't seem to be that number at all. There's -- something quite different is coming up. The number we got was 2663 but that doesn't seem to be the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's 1D. The transcript showed P. Yes, all right. That explains it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That's my mistake. I got carried away. It's Defence Exhibit 1D -- thank you to Mr. Stewart, apologies to the Bench and everybody else for the confusion. Does everybody now have the document? The reference is on the final page of the translation marked 7 of 7 where Mr. Mile Akmadzic speaks. And he says, "With respect to financial help, we are in big trouble. We are practically printing money. We are in serious situation and I think that we will have to put this on the agenda." Ejup Ganic says, "Last time when I was there, I saw Croatia. The exchange rate went 50 per cent up." And Mile Akmadzic says, "We devaluate the Croatian currency. We devaluate the Croatian dinars, that is to say Herzegovina, the area from where the Croatian dinars comes from." Now, sir, my question to you on this and this was just after you left the government or your position, but it seems to me that the Croatian dinars present within Bosnia and Herzegovina was creating certain troubles for the government. Do you read this like that as well or could you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to comment on someone else's statements, people who are not sufficiently familiar with the area but I'll still make a couple of observations. The Croatian dinar was also a provisional currency at the time. After gaining independence, Croatia introduced the Croatian dinar. It was at first a monetary coupon, the same as that issued by the BH government except it was designed much more beautifully, the pattern was better, the paper was much better quality. I can show you the bank note bearing the signature of the minister of finance of Croatia not the governor of the national bank. It was the ministry of finance that produced this provisional currency. It couldn't issue the permanent currency at the time for several reasons. It didn't have the foreign currency reserves and it couldn't make sure the monetary system would be working in a legal way and all this money that was making it to Bosnia and Herzegovina was money that did not have a set value. It was more valuable than the Bosnian dinar otherwise the republic would not have it, but it was a provisional currency. And if you track down the serial numbers of all notes those bank notes you can check that. The money lost value. The Bosnian did and the Croatian money did not so quickly, not at the same pace, not so dramatically but it did. And in 1994, Croatia replaced this provisional currency by a new permanent currency, the Croatian dinar and this was issued by the Croatian National Bank and that's how long the official Croatian currency has been in existence -- and what people are saying about this money being valued or devalued -- well, certainly, and this went quickly for the reasons that I've just tried to explain.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked yet again to slow down. It is impossible to ensure an accurate record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry again to say it. It may happen that I am really maladroit, but I really -- I couldn't find even in the binder of the Defence that very paper and -- but, again, now I -- the President shows me the other paper that is the Prosecution's but it is where we first didn't find it and we were told that it is a D document, that is Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it assists, it is a D document but the Prosecution have thoughtfully included it as the last document in their file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I see. Yes. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm waiting for my fellow Judge to find this document. In the meantime, you have just mentioned something new. So far we haven't heard anything about it. You state that the Croatian dinar which was in circulation in Herzegovina then was actually Croatian dinar coupons issued not by the central bank of Croatia but rather by a signature of the finance minister and you state that the Croatian dinar in circulation then which triggered high inflation was not the Croatian dinar in the sense that it was issued by the central bank, it was actually coupons just like you in Sarajevo issued coupons. Is it what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your understanding is correct, Your Honour. If necessary, if I may, I can illustrate this by showing you an actual bank note that I have on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could be interesting for all of us to see that bank note. We'll put that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it might be good to also see the coupons and I can distribute these photocopied exhibits. I was -- I ran out of time yesterday but we have it and this will save me from my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could have made colour copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Next time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead with your comments, witness. What do we have in front of us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the Croatian dinar issued by the Republic of Croatia, signed by the Minister of Finance of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Zoran Jasic. We don't see any reference here to Croatia's National Bank. This is not something that is entirely uncommon. When a country is unable to introduce a permanent currency or maintain its value, if I may, Your Honours, just another three sentences of explanation. When a country introduces money, tries to maintain its value, can try to maintain its value by administrative means by establishing an exchange rate and officially maintaining it but it must have a well-organised system for that purpose. It must have well-established borders, customs, internal circulation, and control. Alternatively, a country can do something else. It can try and maintain the value of its currency by foreign currency reserves. It takes steps in the market by buying or keeping foreign currency reserves in a bid to preserve the value of its currency. Croatia couldn't do any of those at the time, it couldn't take any of those measures and it decided to start producing provisional money and it went on like that up until 1994, until eventually Croatia introduced its permanent currency because at that point in time it was obvious that they had all the conditions in place for maintaining its value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we see here is a coupon; right? I'm checking the translation. So those 50.000 dinars that we see on the screen, what we see actually is a coupon. The Minister of Finance puts that money into circulation not the Central Bank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. You are entirely right. It's a coupon. It was put into circulation by the Minister of Finance and not by Croatia's National Bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood correctly, you had a second bank note to show us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have Bosnian bank notes on me as well, if you like, and money that we commissioned to be printed. I have Bosnian coupons as well, if you want me to show that, I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have one -- do you have it with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have it on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then you can place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This may be good to also illustrate one of the questions that came from the Bench regarding the stamps and the currency because there was that confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a bank note that was issued by Yugoslavia's National Bank. This is Yugoslav money. It was in circulation in Bosnia and Herzegovina up until the 15th or possibly the 17th of August, 1992. In my evidence, I tried to explain how we were doing our best to limit the influx of this worthless money into Bosnia and Herzegovina. We took a technical step which wasn't very successful. You have an exemplar right in front of you. We ordered that all of the Yugoslav bank notes that were in Bosnia and Herzegovina at a certain point in time should be stamped by the auditing service or the National Bank just to mark them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you have another bank note?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a specimen of the bank note that we commissioned on behalf of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was eventually printed but we were unable to bring it into Bosnia or to put it into circulation for all the reasons that I've explained already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll give exhibit numbers to those documents because the registry was able to take pictures. We'll give Chamber numbers. What about the 50.000 bank note, Madam Registrar, could we have an exhibit number for the first picture which corresponds to the first bank note.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be IC 813.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As for the second bank note, the 1.000 bank note. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IC 814, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third bank note, the specimen bank note with the number 25.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IC 815, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps those IC numbers for the last two numbers could be repeated. They are not picked up on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you please repeat because we do not see that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be numbered IC 813, IC 814, IC 815, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the coupon issued by Bosnia and Herzegovina in August 1992. We were unable to ship the printed bank notes into Sarajevo, the one that was supposed to become our permanent currency and then we had coupons that we used in lieu of money throughout the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll give an IC number as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IC 816, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, when we talk about the Croatian dinar which was being used on the -- in certain areas on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the money that we saw, would that have been the first exhibit that you showed us, the 50.000 dinar bank note or coupon?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, it was a coupon; but in theory and in practice, this was a bank note issued by the Ministry of Finance of the Republic of Croatia and a bank note that had no value as a foreign currency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the use of those coupons outside of Croatia or outside the Republic of Croatia, would that only have been possible with the cooperation of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that was the case. Private individuals got hold of whatever they believed was valuable. I, and anyone else for that matter, as long as I was more inclined that way, could always have chosen to keep in my pocket Croatia's dinar as opposed to perhaps some other currency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Is it correct -- well, we saw that from the last Prosecution Exhibit that -- or sorry, the 1D, the Defence Exhibit 1D 02663, the part or the portion that we looked at, it says, Ejup Ganic says, "I saw that Croatia, the exchange rate went 50 per cent up." Is it correct that the Croatian dinar in 1992 was losing its value?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It was affected by inflation. I'm not sure about the rate but it was affected. I would need to speculate but I would think it was quite a high rate. If I may just to back this up, let me say this. Even in 1993, companies drew up their annual balances and then those needed recalculating because they had to display some more realistic value. The pure monetary value of those balances had been devalued by the inflation rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the value, let's look at Prosecution Exhibit P 09255. That's P, in the Prosecution binder, P 09255.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry I have to find it. Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you page past the first page which is in English, you will see that the next pages consist of copies of the currency exchange rates and starting on the 3rd of February, 1992, and then it goes month-by-month. If you just have a look at that, would that be the currency exchange rate for the Croatian dinar? I know the print is very small.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is the exchange rate. One small correction. This was always published whenever the rate changed so it wasn't on a monthly basis that this was published. There were daily changes sometimes depending on the fluctuating rates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the -- if we could just understand this. If you could look at the list for the 3rd of February, 1992. Can you find the value of the Deutschemark which is marked as DEM?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And those columns, I take it, are for buy, sell, and average?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the value for the Deutschemark as opposed to the dinar would have been -- well, it says -- I can't even read it -- 55.000 -- 550.000, but would that be 55 dinars to a Deutschemark?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less. So although the buy and sell exchange rates differ but we can say that it was about 55 dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you look at the first page, perhaps that English, you will see February 1992 and in the first column, numbers of dinars in one Deutschemark, 55. That would correspond, I take it, to the table that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, could I ask you, perhaps, just very quickly to find the table for December 1992. And for the record, that would be the page number with the number in the top right-hand corner of 04666784 with Vodic beneath it. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, it's an exchange list number one dated 5th January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you could look at the previous page, perhaps, just the previous page. It's the list for Narodna Banka Hrvatske, Zagreb, 1 December 1992. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what was the value of the Deutschemark on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 384 dinars. 384, 385.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look at the first page of the document with the English on, it shows again December 1992, 386, so the point of this, sir, is that is it correct that the Croatian dinar was indeed devaluing or losing its value at a very high rate?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, and I don't wish to be disrespectful to my colleague, but what is the relevance of all of this? I mean I am -- I enjoy the topic I must say, it brings me back to my youthful days when I was in university studying economics but I don't see the relevance in this part of the cross-examination. I really fail to see it. Perhaps he could enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do with respect support that observation. Of course it is cross-examination and whilst we may have time my learned friend of course can lead. It may make us proceed a little faster on these issues because they appear to be without controversy even if they are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, with that table, it is obvious that throughout the month, the Croatian dinar was losing value with respect to the Deutschemark. On the 27th of May, 1994, the value was 3.716. So everybody understands that as months go by, the Croatian dinar loses its value. In order to save time, maybe you could just ask your question. Everybody can see that. But what are you getting at?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm stepping off this topic. It does have relevance but I won't belabour it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to step on to a different document now and this is Prosecution Exhibit P 00476.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, you said 476 but what I have is 467. Is that one and the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I may just assist, this is the document which was not in the binder and that we circulated this morning, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this is an extract from the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina dated 18 December 1992, and it's a decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a decision held on 14 September 1992 and the court rendered the following decision. It says: "The following shall be annulled. The decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna adopted on 18 November by democratically-elected representatives of the Croatian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." And then a number of other decisions and decrees also are listed which are annulled by the Constitutional Court. Now, sir, at this stage on the 14th of September, you were still in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Sarajevo on the 14th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That was the day before your 55th birthday, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know very well my biography.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you in the government aware of this matter being dealt with by the Constitutional Court?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally wasn't aware, but I do not rule out the possibility that someone else knew about it. I see this document for the first time. It was not discussed in the government while I was in Sarajevo. If this decision was taken on the 14th, it did not reach the government by the end of working hours on the 17th or 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the Constitutional Court was still functioning and a legal body at that stage?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are asking me as an ordinary citizen, I'm not a lawyer, I think it was a legal body functioning throughout the whole period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we can very quickly step to another document, P 10506. P 10506 this is actually a document that we have seen previously. Sorry, I think in light of the time constraints we've already dealt with most of the issues which I wanted to touch upon through that document.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm again having problems with documents. I cannot find this document here in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Don't worry, sir, I'm not going to deal with that document now. Actually, no, sorry, there is one aspect so if we could find it, 10506. Now, sir, this is an interview by Zdravko Latal with yourself and was published in Delo on the 20th of August, 1992. Do you recall this interview?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had many interviews with journalists at the time. I don't remember this specific one but I do not rule out the possibility that it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, at the end of the first paragraph, it says, "Finance Minister Dr. Zarko Primorac stated what kind of attitude his state has towards foreign currencies on its territory ..." so that's what this interview was about just to help you orient yourself. If we go to the -- about the fourth paragraph where you talk, Primorac: "We finally put the money into circulation." Do you have that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I only have the Slovenian original and I cannot understand fully the Slovenian language so I cannot grasp the essence of this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, there is one aspect that I would like to in that paragraph take up with you. If I just read to you from the English translation and perhaps you could feel comfortable to comment on it. Referring to the institution of the BH dinar, it says, "Of course we had difficulties in transporting the money to the liberated territories but we overcame those difficulties." Could you, perhaps, just comment on what that would mean?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained yesterday that the government's intention, not its decision but it was just a working agreement to have the dinars printed in Slovenia, shipped and stored at the vault of the National Bank of Croatia and that is what was done. The idea was then to introduce the money into circulation formally and practically in Sarajevo as the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina which I also found to be quite normal. At the same time, we planned that once we put the money into circulation in Sarajevo, to have part of the money shipped to Livno to cover the area of central Bosnia and Herzegovina and another storage in Tuzla and Zenica. Since some confusion set in, this money probably didn't reach these other areas. I don't know what is exactly said in this interview. I did not authorise or authenticate this interview. It was translated from Croatian into Slovenian then from Slovenian into English and then back to me from English into Croatian. Therefore, I would like to see this interview in the Croatian language to know exactly what I said in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I won't continue with this one because you will be at a disadvantage not being able to follow it but I think we've dealt with most of those aspects. Sir, I would like to, in nearly concluding on the Croatian dinar and my cross-examination, just want to test you on this. The presence of the Croatian dinar on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but then more specifically its presence on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was not driven by pragmatic needs but was more driven by ideology and politics. Could you comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this a statement because it's put as if it's a statement of fact. Now, perhaps my learned friend would like to put the inflection at the end of that declarative statement making it thus a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I can assist, I'm putting to the witness that that is indeed the case and I would like his comment thereon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, in money matters, as well as any other material matters of every individual, there is not much importance attached to ideology and national feeling. People want to earn money and be financially stable. If anyone in Bosnia and Herzegovina or elsewhere decided to adopt the Croatian dinar instead of some other currency, they probably had some underlying pragmatic reasons and please bear in mind that at the time, there was no Bosnian-Herzegovinian currency in BH. We did introduce the Bosnian dinar and we had all the decisions in place. We did print it but it wasn't physically there and I quite understand the interest of certain people to use the currency that they had at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the last document that I would like to show you is P 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Yes, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for two hours, we've been listening --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, yesterday, I listened to you and in my view, it was not pertinent, your statement what you made, your questions, rather, what you asked from the witness. Now I would like to know about what would you like to say. Are you also a financial expert? We know that you know about everything but I would like to -- you to explain what is your specialty in finance? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you do not accept the relevance of my yesterday's questions. I said I would explain them later because this tackles the interality [as interpreted] of the financial aspect of this whole affair. This -- hasn't anyone asked this witness who knows perfectly well about these matters what -- the intrusion of the monetary system of Yugoslavia happened, it was Milosevic's order to print 200 or 300 million of US dollars' worth in Yugoslav dinars, that was just banditry. Then you would understand the whole structure. If you, Your Honour, think that I am intervening too often and that I'm trying to be smart, I have education in finances. I can declare this money to be Praljak's money and nobody can buy anything with it. Everyone knows that no value can be declared by any political action. Money is an expression of a value of certain manufactured goods. For three hours now we have been listening to A, B, C, that one can learn in every high school that somebody in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina would declare simple paper to be worth and valuable and on the other hand, you cannot buy flour or anything with it, then how can they sell flour for the worthless money. So I would like to ask you to ask Dr. Primorac to explain why did they stamp the bank notes and did Milosevic engage the mint in Topcider to print the money around the clock in order to pay the bills of Serbia and its citizens and to rob Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia as a highwayman and after that, these two republics in order to prevent this robbery resorted to printing their own money and this is how the whole cycle began. Your Honour, as a sociologist, I have studied economy enough in order to understand these issues about foreign exchange remittance from people working abroad so, please, do not discount me in advance by asking me what are you doing here? Please listen first to my reasons, to the facts that I have to tell you and how I put these facts together and only then I ask you to make your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak. You will receive today the decision of the Chamber about the issue of your role in cross-examination, et cetera, and therefore I now -- I'm not commenting your statement which was a statement, of course, and you have the right to make it. But again, I say that in this particular instance, I do not think that you are an expert in those issues which we are now listening to and talking about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I have only one more document that I want to deal with with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can have a look at Prosecution Exhibit P 10507. P 10507. Immediately, I can tell you that you would probably not have seen these handwritten minutes previously. You would probably not have been at any such meeting because this is after you have left the government. Nevertheless, I'd like to ask you about one or two things in this. It's the 217th Session of the Presidency of the RBiH. It's the minutes for the 4th of October, 1993. If you look on the first page of the minutes, item 3, the second paragraph of item 3, it then deals with governor of the National Bank. Then it says -- do you have that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's the second page of the document, the first page where there's writing and it is right at the end of the -- that page and in the B/C/S, on the first page and there is an item 3 and then a bracket. And just beneath that bracket I think it says, "Governor of the national bank."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, it then says "Stiepo Andrijic absent. Absent for," and then crossed out, "more than a year. A longer period of time from the republic. The government cannot get valid information from the bank about debiting the account of the bank for the orders and in," and then unclear, perhaps, Celje, "and Zagreb. It is not known why the foreign currency has been debited. Stiepo is removed due to the failure to perform his duty in a regular manner." Could you perhaps just comment on this last matter, you having worked with Mr. Stiepo Andrijic, did you have problems with him in his performing his functions as governor of the central bank or the national bank?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I give you a direct answer, allow me a comment. It says at the top that the meeting was attended by Izetbegovic, Dr. Ljujic, Dr. Pejanovic, Hasan Efendic, Lazovic, Djuricic, Djapara [phoen] and Pusina. I do not see the name of the prime minister here or anyone who can say below in the text that the government cannot get valid information from the bank about certain matters. Apparently this is a situation where we have someone speaking on behalf of the government and we do not see the prime minister here. Secondly, I worked with Stipe Andrijic, we studied together economics in Sarajevo. I was not his supervisor and I have to repeat that the central bank just like any country was independent in Bosnia and Herzegovina but on certain issues we did have to cooperate. Never before nor during this brief period of time had I had any problems in my work with Mr. Stipe Andrijic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, sir, it was indeed the government that had to deal with this kind of issue, the government being the members of the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you properly. You said they had to deal or they did not have to deal?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was this something which actually fell within the remit of the government to deal with?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see a lot of details here that I can probably explain to the Chamber that you probably are not able to notice because this is from my domain of expertise. It mentions here the removal of money from bank accounts for payment orders in Celje. Probably, and this is just my guess and assumption, this probably refers to the payments for the printing of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian money that we spoke at length today that was printed in Celje because there were no other relations with Celje other than this one at the time. Further on, it says that it is not known what the foreign exchange currency was paid for and if I -- if this was about Celje, it was for this purposes that I explained. As for Andrijic failing to perform his duties, this is not my remit but when you are talking about the central bank you are not talking about a specific individual, you are talking about the confidence in the bank and the money that it has to take care of. So I find this to be very unusual and I would like to say that I haven't seen this paper before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The final thing then on the next page, we see that Lazovic speaks. And about three lines down he says, "Proposals for decisions to fulfill these three vacant posts with previous removal of Boras and Lasic. Their resignation results from their inclination towards Herceg-Bosna and accepting posts in the Herceg-Bosna and they have not taken active part in the PRBiH for a long time. They took active part in establishing HB." Then there's a quote, Boras and it says, "Centuries' old wish of the Croatian people to have its own state is coming true." Were you aware of people in the government who held such ambitions or who were, as it says here, "Inclined towards Herceg-Bosna"?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have no need or indeed any intention to comment on Mr. Lazovic's observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, is it that you cannot comment on this or does this have some merit in it what is --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, you're asking me to comment on something someone said 15 years ago somewhere that I wasn't physically present and at a meeting of a body of which I was not a member. This would boil down to mere speculation. I'm a serious witness. I'm here to tell you what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, thank you very much. I do agree with you that you are a serious witness and I appreciate your cooperation. Thank you very much, Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prior to the break I just have a very short question. As a result of Mr. Praljak's intervention, yesterday, or was it the day before yesterday, I asked something about the conversion of the Yugoslav dinar that was reduced to a ratio of 10:1 by a decision of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I had asked that question because I'm trying to understand what that meant and now Mr. Praljak intervened, he should not have, but anyway, he said that Mr. Milosevic had indeed printed money and had flooded Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia with Yugoslav dinars and in Mr. Praljak's view, all that had had repercussions among which, I wonder, this one. Given the inflation because the apparition of Yugoslav dinars, did the BH government in order to try and cope with this massive influx of Yugoslav dinars, what did it do? Was a possibility to depreciate the currency in a drastic fashion by a factor of 10? Was that a reason that prompted you, you or the government, to take that step?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is another technical step. It was a technical step which had both a practical meaning and a psychological impact. The practical one, we simply didn't have to print as much money as we had to previously and we were under all sorts of restrictions at the time. We said that the psychological impact is very important when it comes to money so the meaning was to show people that the new BH money had more value than the old one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to break for 20 minutes and then we'll have the redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Mr. Karnavas, I'd like to give the floor to Madam Registrar who is to give us an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the OTP has submitted to its objections to documents tendered by 2D with witness Akmadzic, Mile. The documents tendered will have the IC number 813 [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor for redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I just have one question, really. You were asked today about, or you were told, basically that your primary contacts were with Mr. Turajlic who was vice-president of the government; do you recall being asked that question by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just to be clear that I understand it and that we understand it, Mr. Turajlic was one of three vice-presidents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And each vice-president would coordinate with various ministers depending on their remit; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when it concerned the ministry of finance, it would be up to the vice-president Turajlic, that was within his remit, he was dealing with such matters?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was coordinating the work of all the ministries dealing with the economy, the ministry of industry, trade, traffic, finance and maybe some other ministries that had to do with the country's economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it based on your contacts with Mr. Turajlic, he would then coordinate with the other vice-presidents and then I guess the whole government, essentially, would be coordinating with each other; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As long as that was necessary. As a rule, proposals and issues would be raised at government meetings that had gone through all the coordination levels already, the economic one, the social one and then they would discuss it. Did the coordination people have another coordination meeting before this was tabled to the government, I wouldn't know. I wouldn't say so, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But would it be fair to say or to conclude that based on your contacts with Mr. Turajlic then, the other responsible members of the government and in particular, say, the president of the government and the other ministers would become acquainted with what, if anything, you were doing and you were reporting to Mr. Turajlic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be entirely normal. What I have been talking about doesn't just have to do with the ministry of finance, it had to do with the work of the government as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I want to thank you again very, very much for coming here to give your evidence. Mr. President and Your Honours, I have no further redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Witness, on behalf of my fellow Judges, I would like to thank you for coming here, asked by the Prlic Defence. Thank you for having testified on matters which were within your remit. I'd like to wish you a safe trip home and I wish you all the best in your new position. Mr. Usher will escort you out of this courtroom. Please do not forget your bank notes which are in your bag.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the money is valuable in terms of these being a rare specimen of what it looked like a long time ago. I would like to take this opportunity to thank everyone, the Chamber, the Defence, the Prosecution. I will only be too glad if my evidence contributed to the establishment of truth in this trial. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Registrar would like to correct a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correction, the OTP objections will have the number IC 817.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. We are early today, that's very rare. I seize this opportunity to inform you of the following. Next week, we have a Defence expert witness for the Praljak Defence; is that so, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true, Your Honour. Everything is going forward as planned, the expert will be here on Monday. Actually he arrived today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to that witness, the Chamber has decided that the Praljak Defence will have an hour for their examination in chief. As for the other accused, they will be granted 30 minutes for cross-examination and the Chamber decided that the Prosecution will have two hours all included in order to cross-examine that expert witness. You heard earlier that Judge Prandler mentioned a decision by the Chamber, a decision which will be filed today with respect to cross-examination. I therefore invite all parties to read that decision which was taken in the majority. I personally dissented on the substance of the decision. You are therefore invited to read the said decision. Examination in chief will start on Tuesday. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we adjourn for the weekend, Your Honour, I just wanted to make sure that the Trial Chamber understands that we will not have a witness subsequent to this expert. We were unable to bring one so -- but I did also want to take this opportunity to inform the Trial Chamber that the witness that will follow the expert, our next witness, we have asked for six hours and we understand that others may be -- will, in fact, be questioning the gentleman and so we anticipate that his testimony will last more than one week. We are making provisions so we don't fall behind but -- so that everything is in order from that aspect but we do wish to point out that we have asked for six hours and we believe that it's going to be a Herculean effort to accomplish our task in six hours, just to inform Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, you should tell your witness that, unfortunately, he will have to stay on Monday or Tuesday if you have those six hours, it is up to you. You need to settle the issue with the witness. Having said that, his schedule may necessitate that he comes back at a later stage. The witness should not be put in a position when he's told at the very last minute that he has to stay over the weekend. It can be very unpleasant for him. So please make sure he understands that you can calculate the time very precisely but when the Bench asks questions, it is very difficult to anticipate what will happen. So we trust that you will do the necessary for that. I said that the Prosecutor would have two hours. I do not have the document in front of me. The legal officer tells me it's maybe an hour and a half but you will be informed in due time. Anyway, we will have time and for once, the Judges will not be rushed so we'll have a quiet week and we can put all the questions to the expert. Is there anything you want to raise. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to remind everyone in relation to the next witness that Mr. Karnavas has talked about, we have submitted a motion for this to be a 92 ter witness. We asked for, I think, five or six minutes more in relation to our original request. Maybe we can save up on time and we might use this witness to tender some exhibits into evidence but I'm not talking about a substantial amount of time, maybe up to 20 minutes for direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... 92 ter procedure we will be doing what we've done so far. Examination in chief, cross-examination, and then your witness will be coming back pursuant to 92 ter. That will solve all the problems. Are there any matters to be raised? Nobody wishes to raise anything? Mr. Scott, you are very silent today. No questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure everyone appreciates my silence and I'll leave it at that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I wish you all a nice afternoon. We shall reconvene on Monday afternoon.
